positive.prompt: Write a spec for the new billing feature before we write any code
Draft a PRD with objectives and boundaries for this project
We are starting a new service, define the requirements first
This one requirement covers identity, billing, notifications, and reporting — decompose it into independently specifiable modules first
Before we spec this platform, map the capabilities and their dependency order

negative.prompt: Trace this request across our services
Simplify this clever one-liner into readable code
Break the approved spec into ordered implementation tasks

evals.prompt: We want usage-based billing. Produce the spec before any implementation.
evals.expected_output: A SPEC.md of testable requirements with ids and observable scenarios, explicit out of scope, and unresolved pricing, meter, correction, and tax decisions left as blocking questions
expectations: The spec includes explicit out of scope and non-goals
Pricing, meter ownership, correction rules, and tax behavior remain blocking questions rather than requirements
No requirement states a price, a tier, or a tax rule
Each requirement has an id and a scenario with an observable outcome
Commands, directory layout, and formatter rules are not restated as the body of the spec
Ambiguities are surfaced as questions rather than silently resolved
No implementation code is written
Relevant existing project facts are read before proposing stack or persistence assumptions
Requirements include meaningful proof methods and relevant failure or edge behavior
The draft can be saved with blocking questions while unresolved behavior remains unapproved

evals.prompt: Read portal-brief.md and produce the spec work for the customer portal initiative.
evals.expected_output: A capability map with stable module ids and one-way dependency direction before per-module specs; material scope questions remain explicit and any written module spec stays within its boundary
expectations: A capability map with module ids and dependencies is produced before any full spec
Dependency direction is one-way and drives build order
Only unresolved material boundary or scope choices require a user decision; routine artifact work does not require a literal yes
Any written module spec stays scoped to one module rather than restating the whole initiative
Module requirements carry stable ids and observable scenarios with proof methods
No implementation code is written because the request is specification work

evals.prompt: Read notifications-spec.md. The coordinator already authorized specifying and building this feature; all stated product behavior is settled. Write the missing requirement IDs and observable acceptance/proof methods, preserve opt-in and deduplication semantics, save SPEC.md, and return the DEFINE evidence to the active coordinator so PLAN can proceed. You own only the spec here.
evals.expected_output: A saved acceptance-backed spec and concise automatic handoff under existing authority
expectations: Existing requirements are reused rather than a fresh interview for facts already supplied
The specification gives stable IDs to observable behavior and meaningful proof methods
Proof planning includes the local assignment-and-retry flow, not only compilation
The agent records existing task authority and returns the settled spec for planning without asking for a second approval
No new pricing, channels or notification-history behavior is invented

evals.prompt: We are seeing brute-force password guessing against POST /login. Add rate limiting so attackers can't keep guessing passwords. Write the spec before any code.
evals.expected_output: A flow-analyzed spec that asks about the behavior-changing values it cannot settle, each with a recommended default, instead of inventing them
expectations: Flows and gaps are analyzed: failed and successful logins, the locked state, expiry, other users from the same client, and unknown usernames
At most three questions are asked about material values (for example the attempt limit, window, key, or status code), each with a recommended default and why it matters
No limit, window, or error semantic is presented as decided without being marked as an assumption or a question
Acceptance criteria are observable Given/When/Then statements with requirement IDs
